## Overview

The Wolof (*Wolof*, self-designation; *Ouolof* or *Jolof* in older French sources) are a West African people of the Senegambian coastal plain, the largest ethnic group in Senegal and a substantial minority in the Gambia and southern Mauritania, with a diaspora concentrated in France, Italy, Spain and the United States. Their language, also called *Wolof*, belongs to the Atlantic (Senegambian) branch of the Niger-Congo family and functions as the de facto national lingua franca of Senegal, spoken as a first or second language by a majority of the country's population. Estimates for the Wolof proper range from roughly seven to nine million, with tens of millions more using the language across the sub-region. Historically their identity coalesced around the medieval Jolof Empire (c. 1350–1549) and its successor states — Kajoor, Bawol, Waalo, Sine and Saloum — polities structured by a stratified order of nobles (*géer*), casted artisans and praise-singers (*ñeeño*), and formerly enslaved dependants (*jaam*). In folk-culture terms the Wolof matter as the great tailors, goldsmiths and griots of the Atlantic coast: the flowing *boubou* silhouette and its indigo and embroidery traditions, the filigreed gold of the Dakar and Saint-Louis *bijoutiers*, the reverse-glass painting called *sous-verre*, and above all the *sabar* drum ensemble — inscribed together with related Senegalese percussion practice on national heritage lists and widely propagated through the popular *mbalax* idiom — all sit within their tradition.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Indigo dyeing** (*gara* or *teinture à l'indigo*) — the resist-dyeing of locally woven or imported cotton in vats of fermented *Indigofera* leaves, producing the deep blue-black cloth (*sër u nit ku ñuul*) prized for wrappers and men's boubous; stitch-resist, tie-resist and stencilled paste-resist techniques are all used, with Saint-Louis and the Waalo river towns historically renowned centres.

**Batik and *teinture*** — a twentieth-century adaptation using imported wax and chemical dyes, worked by women's cooperatives in Dakar, Thiès and Rufisque; the "batik Senegal" of the tourist and export market descends from this practice and combines wax-resist blocks with tie-dye (*plangi*) rosettes.

**Strip-woven cloth** (*pagne tissé*, in Wolof *sër u ràbb*) — narrow warp-faced bands roughly ten to twenty centimetres wide, woven by men on a horizontal double-heddle loom and sewn edge-to-edge into wrappers and blankets; the finest pieces incorporate weft-float geometric patterning and are commissioned for weddings and naming ceremonies.

**Embroidery** (*broderie*) — dense chain-stitch and couched-cord embellishment of the neck opening, chest panel and cuffs of the *grand boubou*, worked in silk or rayon thread on damask (*bazin riche*); Wolof tailors of Dakar's Sandaga quarter and of Saint-Louis have made this the signature decorative surface of Senegalese formal dress.

***Bazin riche*** — heavily starched and beetled cotton damask, imported in bolts and then dyed, stitched and calendered locally to a mirror-bright finish; the calendering (*battage*) is done by teams of women beating the folded cloth with wooden mallets.

**Motif vocabulary.** Lozenges and interlace of clear Sahelian origin; the *khasa* checkerboard borrowed from Fulɓe weavers; stylised kola nuts, cowries, cola-flower rosettes; calligraphic Arabic devices along collar and pocket embroidery, often reduced to abstract knots when the tailor is not literate in Arabic script; the star-and-crescent as a Sufi and national reference.

### Clothing & dress

The signature Wolof garment is the *mbubb* — in French *boubou* — a wide unfitted robe cut from a single width of cloth folded at the shoulder, with a boat neckline and a large embroidered chest pocket. Men pair the *grand boubou* over matching drawstring trousers (*tubay*) and a long tunic (*caftan*), finished with embroidered leather slippers (*mparaka*) and a small brimless cap (*mbàkk* or *kufi*); marabouts and elders wind a turban (*tenge*) over the cap. Women wear an ankle-length wrapper (*sër*) with a fitted or loose top (*ndoket*) and, for ceremonies, the towering starched headtie (*musóor*), tied into fan and shell shapes whose names change season by season; the *taalibe* boubou of unbleached cotton is worn by Quranic students, and the *ndoket-sër-musóor* trio in matching *bazin* remains the standard formal ensemble for weddings, baptisms and Tabaski. Skin-lightening, gold-thread eyeliner and, for brides, elaborate henna (*fudden*) on hands and feet are part of the same aesthetic system; the *thiouraye* incense mixture perfumes cloth and body together, and the beaded waist-strings (*bin-bin* or *ferr*) worn under the wrapper are an intimate marker of adult femininity.

### Architecture

The Wolof were, and largely remain, villagers and townspeople of the sandy Sahelian coast rather than builders of monumental stone. The traditional rural compound (*kër*) is a walled or fenced enclosure of round mud-and-thatch huts (*neeg*) with conical millet-stalk roofs, one hut per adult woman, arranged around a swept sand courtyard shaded by a *palaver tree* — often a kapok or tamarind — under which the male head of household receives guests. In the historic towns of Saint-Louis and Gorée, Wolof (and Métis *signare*) households adopted the Franco-Iberian creole townhouse: two-storey coral-rubble and lime-plaster buildings with wooden shuttered galleries and interior courtyards, a hybrid form which UNESCO recognises in the World Heritage inscriptions of *Île de Saint-Louis* and *Île de Gorée*. Sufi cities such as Touba (Mouride) and Tivaouane (Tijaniyya) developed a distinct modern religious architecture of white-plastered mosques with squared minarets and green-tiled domes, of which the Great Mosque of Touba is the emblem. Nomadic architecture does not apply — the Wolof have been sedentary agriculturalists and traders throughout the historical period.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Wolof pottery is women's work, done without a wheel by coil-building and paddle-and-anvil finishing, fired in open bonfires of grass and dung; the characteristic products are the wide-mouthed water jar (*ndaa*), the couscous steamer (*cin*), and small incense burners (*cuuraay*) for burning *thiouraye*. Metalwork belongs to the casted *tëgg* (smiths), historically both feared and indispensable: iron hoes and knives, brass and aluminium cooking pots recycled from scrap, and above all the silver and gold work of the *tëgg u wurus* (goldsmiths) of Saint-Louis, Dakar and Kaolack, whose *orfèvrerie sénégalaise* is discussed below. Leatherwork (*wet*) is a separate casted craft (*uude*): tooled and dyed sheath scabbards, sandal soles, saddle fittings, Quran satchels, and the small square amulet-cases (*téeré*) that hold written *gris-gris*. Calabash gourds are pyroengraved with geometric bands and used as bowls, dippers and drum resonators. Reverse-glass painting (*sous-verre*, in Wolof *suweer*) is a distinctive urban folk art that emerged in Saint-Louis and Dakar in the late nineteenth century under North African influence: pigments and ink are applied to the back of a pane of glass in reverse sequence — outlines first, backgrounds last — producing brightly coloured scenes of Sufi saints (especially Cheikh Amadou Bamba), market types, wrestlers, and Quranic episodes.

**Signature crafts (list form, exceptional).**

- ***Sous-verre* / reverse-glass painting** — Saint-Louis and Dakar workshops; Sufi hagiography and street-life scenes.
- **Filigree goldsmithing** (*filigrane*, *xuur*) — twisted and granulated wire earrings, pendants and bracelets in 18k gold.
- **Wolof pottery** — hand-built, open-fired water and cooking vessels; women's craft.
- **Leather amulet-cases** (*téeré*) — square or cylindrical, holding folded Quranic *gris-gris*.
- **Calabash pyroengraving** — geometric bands, used as bowls and drum resonators.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Senegalese goldsmithing is one of the great West African metal traditions and the Wolof *tëgg u wurus* its principal exponents. The characteristic technique is filigree (*filigrane*): fine gold or silver wires drawn to hair-thinness, twisted, coiled into rosettes and half-moons, and soldered onto a plain sheet or open framework, often further textured by granulation. Signature forms include the openwork *boucles* earrings of Saint-Louis with dangling teardrop pendants, the multi-strand twisted-wire torque, the filigree bangle (*jaaro*) worn stacked, and the heavy hollow-worked "cathédrale" pendant developed for the nineteenth-century *signare* clientele and still made for weddings. Coral, amber and Venetian glass trade beads (*cauris* and *ferr*) are strung with gold spacers; the beaded waist-string (*bin-bin*) is beaded by women and worn intimately. Amulets (*gris-gris*, *téeré*) — small leather-wrapped packets containing Quranic verses or herbal preparations prescribed by a *sëriñ* — are worn on necklaces, arm-cords and belts, and are considered protective rather than ornamental, though the two categories overlap in practice. Henna and *khôl* eyeliner (*xuur*) round out the ceremonial toilette; scarification, once practised by older generations as small cheek and temple marks, is now rare among urban Wolof.

## Music & performance

The Wolof soundscape is dominated by the *sabar*, an ensemble of goblet-shaped single-headed drums played with one bare hand and one thin curved stick, tuned by pegs driven into the goat-skin head. The ensemble is hierarchical: the lead *nder* (tall, high-pitched) improvises against a battery of supporting *mbëng-mbëng*, *tungune*, *talmbat* and the deep *lamb*, with the low bass *gorong* anchoring the pattern. Sabar is played by casted *géwël* (griot) drummers at *tànnibéer* neighbourhood dances, weddings, wrestling matches and political rallies, and its rhythms — *baar mbay*, *ceebu jën*, *yaaba*, *farwu jaar* — have names and choreographies that dancers are expected to recognise on the first bar. The related *tama* (small hourglass talking-drum, squeezed under the arm to bend pitch) and the *xalam* (a small plucked lute with two to five strings, ancestral to the banjo) accompany the sung praise poetry (*taasu*, *woy*) of the *géwël*. In the twentieth century these elements were fused with Cuban son and rock instrumentation into *mbalax*, the popular idiom of Youssou N'Dour, Baaba Maal, Thione Seck and Omar Pene, which is now the mainstream popular music of Senegal. Sufi devotional song — the Mouride *khassaïd* chanted from the poetry of Cheikh Amadou Bamba, and the Tijaniyya *mawlid* and *sikkar* — occupies a parallel sacred sphere.

## Dance & theatre

Sabar dance (*fecc*) is the signature performance genre: explosive, high-kicking, deliberately provocative solos in which women (and, in the *tànnibéer* context, primarily women) enter the ring one at a time to answer the lead drum's phrases with named steps — *ventilateur*, *farwu jaar*, *baar mbay*. The dance is understood as competitive and flirtatious, and its erotic charge is part of its social meaning; in a religious frame the same body vocabulary reappears in the *ndëpp* healing ceremony, where possession by *rab* spirits is induced and negotiated through rhythm. Wrestling (*làmb* or *làmb ji*) is treated as a hybrid sport and theatre: bouts are preceded by lengthy *bàkk* self-praise chants, amulet-binding, and processions of drummers, and the champions (*mbër*) are cultural celebrities of the first rank. Masked performance is comparatively marginal among the Wolof proper — the great Senegalese mask traditions belong to the Diola of Casamance and the Bassari of the southeast — but the *kankurang* initiation masquerade, inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, circulates in Wolof-Mandinka border zones of the Gambia and Saloum. Urban francophone theatre (Sorano stage, Dakar) and *set-setal* street pageantry are the modern continuations.

## Festivals & rituals

The life-cycle rituals are the armature of Wolof social time. The naming ceremony (*ngente*) is held on the seventh day after birth: the child's head is shaved, the name is whispered into its ear by an elder, a sheep is sacrificed, and *thiéboudienne* is served to the neighbourhood; griots deliver praise poetry in exchange for gifts of cloth and cash. Circumcision (*xaraf*) of boys, historically a bush retreat with masked instructors, is now largely a hospital procedure followed by a home celebration. Marriage (*céet*) unfolds over multiple stages — *warugar* bride-price negotiation, the religious *takk* at the mosque, and the *xew* public feast — and is the principal occasion for the display of matching *bazin* boubous and filigree gold. Funerals (*dëj*) are simple by Islamic prescription but followed by a forty-day mourning and Quranic recitation. The Islamic calendar overlays this with *Korité* (Eid al-Fitr) and *Tabaski* (Eid al-Adha, the great sheep feast), and the Sufi orders add the vast annual pilgrimages: the *Màggal* of Touba, commemorating Cheikh Amadou Bamba's 1895 exile, draws several million Mourides each year and is the largest single religious gathering in Senegal; the *Gàmmu* of Tivaouane marks the Prophet's birthday for the Tijaniyya.

## Foodways

The Wolof national dish, and by extension Senegal's, is *ceebu jën* — "rice and fish" — a one-pot preparation of broken rice cooked in a tomato and *néré*-seasoned fish broth with stuffed fish (usually *thiof*, white grouper) and a medley of cassava, carrot, cabbage, aubergine (*jaxatu*, bitter tomato), and okra, served with tamarind or lime and a spoonful of *xoñ* (fermented condiment); it was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2021 as *"Ceebu Jën, culinary art of Senegal"*. Other core dishes include *yassa* (chicken or fish marinated in lemon, mustard and onions), *maafe* (peanut-butter stew), *thiéré* (steamed millet couscous with baobab-leaf sauce, *soow* fermented milk, or peanut sauce), *fataya* and *pastels* (fried stuffed pastries of Portuguese descent), and the ubiquitous shared platter eaten with the right hand around a single enamelled bowl. Drinks include *bissap* (hibiscus infusion), *bouye* (baobab-fruit drink), *ginger* (spiced ginger juice), *café Touba* (coffee spiced with *djar* pepper, a Mouride signature), and the three-round green-tea ritual (*ataaya*), poured from height to build the foam and drunk in sequence from bitter to sweet.

## Oral tradition & literature

Oral literature is the domain of the casted *géwël* (griot), who function as genealogist, praise-singer, historian and diplomatic intermediary. The core repertoires are *taasu* — rhythmic recited praise poetry, often improvised over a *sabar* pattern and now recognised as an African ancestor of rap — *woy* sung song, and the epic cycles of the Jolof kings, the *linger* queens of Waalo, and the founders of the Sufi orders. Proverb (*léebu*) and riddle (*cakkatuy*) are still the standard rhetorical furniture of adult conversation. Written Wolof exists in two parallel scripts: *Wolofal*, an Arabic-script orthography used since at least the eighteenth century for religious poetry (notably the *khassaïd* of Cheikh Amadou Bamba, whose devotional corpus runs to tens of thousands of verses) and everyday correspondence in rural areas, and a Latin-script orthography standardised by the Senegalese state in 1971 and used in press, primers and modern literature. Ousmane Sembène, Cheikh Anta Diop, Mariama Bâ and Boubacar Boris Diop are the towering modern authors; Diop's novel *Doomi Golo* (2003) is the landmark work of Wolof-language literary prose.

## Language & religion

Wolof is an Atlantic (Senegambian) language of the Niger-Congo phylum, marked typologically by noun-class concord (eight to ten classes depending on analysis), verb-focus and locative morphology, and a rich system of aspectual conjugations rather than tenses. It is the mother tongue of roughly 40% of Senegal's population and the working lingua franca of perhaps 80–90%, spreading at the expense of Serer, Pulaar and Mandinka in urban areas. Two main varieties are distinguished: the prestige Dakar-Saint-Louis Wolof and the Gambian Wolof of the lower river. In religion, the overwhelming majority of Wolof are Sunni Muslims of the Maliki school, and Islam has been embedded in Wolof society since at least the eleventh century, but the specifically Wolof form of it is Sufi and organised around brotherhoods (*tariqa*): the Tijaniyya (with centres at Tivaouane and Kaolack), the Mouridiyya founded by Cheikh Amadou Bamba at Touba in the 1880s, the Qadiriyya, and the Layene of the Lebu fishing community around Dakar. The relationship between *marabout* (*sëriñ*) and disciple (*taalibe*) — pledged obedience in exchange for spiritual guidance and, in the Mouride case, an ethic of work — is the central social institution of contemporary Wolof life, and it is on the fabric of that relationship that the boubou, the filigree, the *sous-verre* portrait of Cheikh Amadou Bamba and the great *Màggal* pilgrimage are all, in different registers, embroidered.
